morph.rootq: §2.6 p.20: 'In Abun, stress is predictable. Stress occurs on the last syllable of each word.' (examples /ye.'bris/ 'male', /no.wa.'rek/ 'lightning', /man.gor.'es/ 'spinach'). The rule is stated over the word, not the root, and the morphology sections apply it across affixes: 'the primary stress occurs on the final syllable and so the prefix, suk-, is unstressed' (§3.3.2.1 p.32); for suffixed ndi-gat 'fight-INT': 'Instead of an independent stress centre on each morpheme the primary stress is on -gat, according to the stress patterns found in Abun words' (§3.3.1.4 p.30); compounds: 'in kapar-ok the final syllable ok is stressed, while the syllables ka and par are not' (§3.3.2.3 p.34).
morph.elicq: No statement of how stress was determined. §2.6 p.20 gives only isolated citation words: 'Stress occurs on the last syllable of each word. The following examples illustrate this. Stress is indicated by ˈ preceding the stressed syllable. /ye.ˈbris/ male, /bo.ˈge/ fish, /kwe.ˈnu/ tree sap, /i.ˈbit/ bad, /no.wa.ˈrek/ lightning, /man.gor.ˈes/ spinach.' Elsewhere prosody is invoked impressionistically as a wordhood test (p.34: 'If this was a clause ... then par of kapar would be stressed and the word ok would have its own independent stress'). No frames, texts or measurements are mentioned for stress.
morph.stmt: 'The Abun language is best classified as an isolating or analytic language... an average morpheme-to-word ratio of 1:1.13... The processes of word-building in Abun are therefore rather limited. The following processes are evident: limited suffixation on verbs (§3.3.1) [-wa, -bot, -ket, -gat]; three prefixes for nouns (§3.3.2) [suk- NOM, ye- PERS, i- 'its']; word compounding, principally in nouns' (§3.1 pp.23-24) — i.e. near-isolating, with the little derivational morphology split: prefixes on nouns, suffixes on verbs, and all inflection-like categories (person, TAM, negation, interrogative, number, possession) carried by free pronouns, particles, classifiers and the linker bi.

tn.quote: Tone in Abun has a low functional load and may be disappearing as a useful contrastive feature. There are three contrastive tones, high/rising, low, and falling. In this section, high or rising tone is marked with an acute accent mark above the vowel of the syllable, falling tone is marked with a grave accent, and low tone is unmarked. ... In example 2.21a /òn/ has a falling tone, whereas in example 2.21c /on/ has a low tone. In example 2.21a /buk/ has a low tone, whereas in 2.21b /búk/ has a rising tone.

ev.text: Words form PHRASES, or stress groups, within utterances. A phrase can be separated from other phrases by pauses and it contains a single stressed word. It is convenient to distinguish two kinds of stress: PHRASE STRESS and WORD STRESS. Phrase stress falls on the stressed word in the phrase (usually the final or penultimate word). Word stress falls on the final syllable of a word. ... This stress is realised when a word is pronounced in its citation form, or when it is the stressed word in a phrase. When a word occurs in an unstressed position in a phrase all its syllables are pronounced unstressed. Such an unstressed word is termed CLITICISED.

The rule is stated on the word, but the grammar ties it to the root explicitly: §3.2.1 p.39 'Since infixation is never into the final syllable of a stem or root and there is no suffixation it should be clear that word final syllables in Acehnese are always mono-morphemic and they represent the final syllable of the root morpheme'; §2.1 p.12 'In Acehnese word stress is upon the final syllable. The phonological form of final syllables is invariant: no morphophonemic rules affect final syllables'; §2.4.1 p.26 and §3.2.1 p.38: prefixes are CV monosyllables of the…
morph.elicq: §3.1.2 p.36: 'This stress is realised when a word is pronounced in its citation form, or when it is the stressed word in a phrase. When a word occurs in an unstressed position in a phrase all its syllables are pronounced unstressed.' (stress analysed at phrase level: §2.4.1 p.26 'Stress in Acehnese is assigned at the level of the phrase'). General method, §1.4 p.10: 'I did relatively little direct elicitation and preferred to collect data from conversations and recorded narrative texts.' No instrumental measurement of stress is reported (ch.2 acoustic data cover VOT, murmur and vowel formants only).
morph.stmt: Exclusively pre-root morphology: 'Although Acehnese has no inflectional morphology - it does not mark for gender, case, person or number - it does have derivational morphology, using prefixation and infixation to form words from other words. There are no suffixes. All prefixed morphemes are monosyllables with a CV segmental structure' (§3.2.1 p.38); argument person is marked by pronominal proclitics (Agent, obligatory) and enclitics (Undergoer/possessor, optional) on the…

contra.head: A 1991 article argues Afrikaans is not an initial-stress language
contra.detail: Wissing 1991 answers De Stadler's (SAJL 9: 41-46) defence of an initial-stress analysis of Afrikaans simplexes and of the objections to Wissing's main-stress rule, which places stress on the penultimate or final syllable. Abstract: 'De Stadler is van mening dat Afrikaans 'n inisiëleklemtoontaal is. Hy kritiseer nie net die hoofklemtoonreël van Wissing, wat die klemtoon basies op die voorfinale of die finale sillabe plaas nie [...]' and 'Die algemene gevolgtrekking waartoe ge-kom is, is dat die Wissing-reël op beskrywende en voorspellende vlak meer doeltreffend is as die klemtoonreël van De Stadler, en dat daar goeie grond is waarop Afrikaans nie as inisiëleklemtoontaal getipeer kan word nie…

Isolated remark: verbs in stressed -eer have 'only a secondary stress on the first syllable' (p. 224 fn.). Restated by Wissing 2020:137 ('secondary stress will be on the second constituent').

morph.rootq: p. 27 §1.10.1: 'In words of Germanic origin the stress is on the first syllable although there are many exceptions to this in certain derived forms'; p. 27 §1.10.1.1: 'There are a number of suffixes (some foreign, but most indigenous) and prefixes which, when added to words, cause the stress to shift to a syllable other than the first'; p. 28 §1.10.1.1.2: 'The verbal prefixes be-, er-, ge-, her-, ont- and ver-, which also occur in nouns derived from such verbs, are never stressed, e.g. bedreig ... verwagting'; p. 30 §1.10.1.1.4: 'Derived adjectives ending in -baar or -lik normally stress the root of the word, but there are long-standing derivatives where the ending has drawn the stress…
morph.elicq: p. 26 §1.10: 'In the analysis of Afrikaans stress patterns given below, the stressed vowel is given in bold type.' The only evidential remark is bibliographic (p. 29 fn.: 'The full story of where to stress words in -agtig is a good deal more complex than this (see Claassens 1987), but this is a reasonably reliable rule of thumb advocated by De Villiers (1987: 161)'); the preface's 'All the examples were collected in the field, so to speak, and have been checked by native-speakers for their grammaticality' (p. xvi) concerns the sample sentences, not stress. No wordlist, frame, text or instrumental basis is stated for the stress rules.
morph.stmt: Donaldson describes a weakly inflecting language whose nominal/adjectival inflection is suffixal (plural -s/-e §4.1, diminutive -tjie §4.2, attributive -e §6.1) but whose only verbal inflection is the participial prefix ge- and whose verb derivation is prefixal: 'there are, with very few exceptions, only two forms of the verb in Afrikaans, the stem/root/base form... and the past participle from which the past tense is formed' (§8.2 p. 218), 'The past participle is formed by prefixing ge- to the stem' (§8.5 p. 223), and 'New verbs are derived from existing verbs by the addition of a limited series of unstressed, inseparable prefixes, namely be-, er-, ge-, her-, ont-, ver-'…

tn.quote: Coetzee et al. (2018) demonstrate that the voicing contrast is collapsing word-initially, with prevoiced plosives being replaced by voiceless (unaspirated) plosives. They also found that the loss of the voicing contrast does not result in a concomitant loss of lexical contrast. Lexical contrast, rather, is preserved on the following vowel, with vowels after historically voiced plosives being realised with a low f0, and those after historically voiceless plosives being realised with a high f0 (i.e. the original voicing contrast is being replaced by a tonal contrast).
tn.cite: Wissing, Daan P. 2020. Afrikaans (Illustrations of the IPA). Journal of the International Phonetic Association 50(1): 127-140. doi:10.1017/S0025100318000269. Section 'Consonants', pp. 130-131.
tn.locator: pp. 130-131, section 'Consonants' (paragraph on plosives, running over the page break)
tn.note: Donaldson 1993 does not discuss tone. Wissing 2020, after Coetzee et al. 2018: word-initial b/d vs p/t voicing is collapsing, the contrast kept as low vs high f0 on the next vowel (incipient tone).

2.cfw: Donaldson (1993) gives first-syllable stress for words of Germanic origin, but the specialist work on Afrikaans stress (Wissing 1989, 2019, 2020), including an acoustic corpus study, puts main stress at the right edge of monomorphemic words (final unless that syllable is unstressable, then penultimate) with initial stress only in compounds, so the fixed-initial coding holds for native simplexes and compounds but not as the word-stress system. One further first-hand description conflicts (see the conflicting-description item); the entry follows Donaldson 1993.

evidence_works.detail: A judgement questionnaire (124 first-year students, 72 polysyllabic nouns read aloud, 'would definitely use / would definitely not use') shows that the choice of Afrikaans diminutive allomorph (-etjie vs -(t)jie/-kie/-pie) and plural allomorph (-e vs -s) depends on whether the final syllable is stressed, against Trommelen's stress-free rime-based account of Dutch. The article gives no rule for where stress falls; it treats stress as lexically given and its sample contains polysyllabic simplex nouns with either initial or final stress (e.g. satan, totem, bloekom vs kanon, kristal, kapel, kokon)

5.dq: In the phonological phrase the basic stress pattern is that of a rapid build up of intensity on the first syllable, and a decay of intensity on the last one to three syllables ... Within words, the penultimate syllable tends to have slightly more stress, and within the phrase marked stress is heard on certain words, usually grammatically predictable.
5.dloc: Sharpe 1972:14 §2.2.0 'Stress Patterns' (Google Books, vol. ZR8YAQAAMAAJ); also p.35 §4.1.5: 'native speaker stress could always be heard as penultimate in the word, and the variations heard could be conditioned by phrase stress interference'
5.prule: Sharpe (1972:34, s.4.1) hears word stress on the penultimate syllable of the stem (the only syllable of one-syllable stems), 'though I do not always hear it in this position': two-syllable stems always penult (máma, núļa; suffixed núļa-ti 'he alone', dúma-wař 'fat' keep the stem stress, off the word penult); three-syllable stems mostly penult though 'a large number' initial (aláwal, balpálpi vs ñúřadi, pářaka); four-syllable stems stress on the first and third syllables, primary hard to decide; five-syllable stems penult or antepenult. Interrogatives are stressed on the penult of the word, not the stem; auxiliary verbs on the first syllable of the auxiliary stem (except the stem apu, and stem-final before -wun); multisyllable words are 'normally penultimate' but a word with a repeated stem part may stress the first syllable of the repeated part. She adds (s.4.1.5) that she suspects stress is predictable within the word and that to the native speaker it 'could always be heard as penultimate in the word'.
5.srule: Sharpe reports secondary stress only by stem length and with hedges: on four-syllable stems stress and secondary stress fall on the first and third syllables (which is stronger is sometimes undecidable); on five-syllable stems primary is heard penult or antepenult with secondary stress on the first syllable. No general rhythmic secondary rule; not entered in the grid.
5.quote: Phrase stress is very marked, and can obscure this word stress. However I tend to hear stress within words as on the penultimate syllable of the stem of the word (or on the only syllable of one syllable stems), though I do not always hear it in this position. 4.1.1 In two syllable stems stress always appears to be penultimate, except that in interrogatives the penultimate syllable of the word is always the one stressed. On three syllable stems stress is mostly on the penultimate syllable ... On five syllable stems, stress tends to be heard penultimate or antipenultimate, with secondary stress…

corr.head: StressTyp2's coding does not match the source
corr.detail: StressTyp2 entry: "Albanian: In words of all sizes, primary stress falls on the penultimate syllable." The source gives: One stress per word form, computed on the base form B of the inflectional paradigm (inflectional suffixes are stress-neutral): stress the final syllable of B if it is closed with a full vowel or has nucleus i/a/u; otherwise stress the penult of B; monosyllabic bases stress their only syllable. Surface position in inflected words therefore ranges from final to 4th-from-last (kum.bu.ll-a.ve). — StressTyp2 codes fixed penultimate at all lengths with no weight sensitivity (citing Hetzer 1978, Gordon 2002).

6.dloc: Coretta, Riverin-Coutlée, Kapia & Nichols 2023, JIPA 53(3):1135, 'Lexical stress'
6.heavy: Base-final syllable attracts stress if it is CLOSED and has a FULL (non-schwa) vowel, or if its nucleus is i, a or u (open or closed); open final syllables in e/o and all final syllables in ë do not attract stress. Only the final syllable of the base is 'visible' for weight/quality. No vowel-length criterion (Tosk has no contrastive length).
6.prule: One stress per word form, computed on the base form B of the inflectional paradigm (inflectional suffixes are stress-neutral): stress the final syllable of B if it is closed with a full vowel or has nucleus i/a/u; otherwise stress the penult of B; monosyllabic bases stress their only syllable. Surface position in inflected words therefore ranges from final to 4th-from-last (kum.bu.ll-a.ve).
6.srule: None: one stress per word form -- 'Basic Features of Albanian Word Stress: 1 stress/word form' (Trommer & Grimm 2004, slide 3; slide 23 'Restriction to 1 Stress': a single right-aligned trochaic foot per prosodic word), restated in Trommer 2013: 'every prosodic word contains only one (monosyllabic or bisyllabic) foot at its right edge'. Coretta et al. 2023: 1135-1137 discuss primary lexical stress only.

evidence_works.detail: Duration is the only reliable acoustic cue to word stress in Kosovo Standard Albanian: stressed vowels are 30-40% longer than unstressed ones (about 3:2 in minimal pairs, 5:3 in read text), while intensity and F0 show no effect and unstressed vowels are not reduced; final open syllables are lengthened regardless of stress. Placement is taken from the literature as morphological (last stem syllable in verbs, penultimate stem syllable in nouns and adjectives, always within the last three syllables), which the catalog's hedged penult rule already reflects, so the article adds phonetic correlates

evidence_works.detail: Accent is fixed through nominal and verbal inflection and usually falls on the last syllable of the derivational stem, with many accent-attracting suffixes as exceptions; the author relays Canalis's (2007) phonetic rule that the penultimate mora is stressed. This is a morphological restatement compatible with the catalog's weight-hedged penultimate rule, not a different position.

evidence_works.detail: The article is an Optimality-Theory (Align-XP, Wrap-XP, Stress-Focus) account of where informative and emphatic focus lands in Albanian sentences, drawn from a corpus of Kosovo broadcast speech (Albania-Serbia 2014 match commentary and the programme Pressing, 30 May 2022); its finding is that focus sits at the right edge in canonical order but is pulled to non-canonical positions by Stress-XP and syntactic restrictions. On word stress it gives one secondhand line (citing Rugova 2019): stress falls on the penultimate mora rather than the penultimate syllable, which is a weight-sensitive formula

6.cfw: Trommer & Grimm 2004, Canalis 2008 and Coretta et al. 2023 agree that Albanian stress falls on the last syllable of the stem when it is closed or ends in a full non-mid vowel and otherwise on the penult, with inflection never moving it, and Newmark et al. 1982 and Matasović 2012 describe the same facts as regular stem-final stress with penultimate exceptions, so the placement is settled and the only disagreement is which case is called the default.

7.caution: Based on an excerpt only; the full text of the source has not been consulted.
7.dq: Words that begin with a vowel have stress on the second syllable, otherwise stress is on the first. Secondary stresses occur on alternating syllables after the main stress but usually not the last. (Yallop 1977)
7.dloc: the StressTyp2 entry (= Yallop 1977, no page given), StressTyp2 words iylˈpa, mˈpula, ˈkwiya, iˈlipa, waˈliymparra, apmˈpirniˌtjika
7.heavy: No rime-weight criterion. What conditions primary stress is the word-initial onset: a word-initial vowel (and initial wa-, yu-, which Yallop treats as complex vowels rather than CV syllables) is skipped and stress goes to 'the first vowel following a consonant'. Gordon 2005 codes this as onset weight CV > (W)V. Vowel length and closed syllables play no role in primary stress; for secondary stress only, Yallop p. 45 notes a class of words where secondary stress 'is shifted forward from a penultimate i to a preceding relatively long a'.
7.dflt: not applicable in rime terms; when the initial syllable is onsetless or glide-initial, stress is peninitial
7.prule: Primary stress on the first vowel following a consonant: consonant-initial words are stressed on the first vowel ('kwatja, 'rinha); vowel-initial words (including wa-/yu-initial, analysed as complex vowels) on the second vowel (a'tha, am'pa, i'lipa, wa'liymparra, yu'kuntja). Under Yallop's alternative abstract analysis (deleted initial vowel in C-initial words) the rule is uniformly 'second vowel'.
7.srule: In longer words a secondary stress (a degree 'intermediate between primary stress and unstressed', p. 35) accompanies the primary on the second vowel: it falls on the penultimate vowel in five-vowel words and on the antepenultimate vowel in words of six or more vowels (apm'pirniˌtjika 'will cook', a'kaltjiˌliyla, a'kngiyaˌlhika; monomorphemic long words follow the same pattern, ng'kwarliˌlanima); in one class of words the secondary instead immediately follows the primary, 'shifted forward from a penultimate i to a preceding relatively long a' (including all five-vowel words with propriative -akirta).

Otherwise, the stress rule, framed in terms of surface phonetic forms, is that stress is assigned to the first vowel following a consonant'; Yallop 1977:35 'Almost always, the phonemic shape of a word is sufficient to indicate which syllables are stressed'. Morphological structure enters only for secondary stress/stress domains: Yallop 1977:44 'Relatively long words which are single morphemes again generally conform to the pattern of suffixed words or…
morph.elicq: Neither the accessible Yallop 1977 passages (pp.13, 35, 43-45, snippet access only) nor Moore 2012 §2.5.1.2 (p.51) says what kind of data the stress observations rest on; Yallop 1977:35 only says 'Almost always, the phonemic shape of a word is sufficient to indicate which syllables are stressed, and the position of primary and secondary stresses will be described in terms of phonological structure'. Moore's corpus in general is 'extensive text collections and data elicitation' (abstract p.3) but this is not tied to his stress remarks.
morph.stmt: 'Alyawarr is agglutinative and suffixing. Noun cases and verb tenses are marked by suffixes.' (Moore 2012 §1.2.1 p.15); 'Alyawarr verbs are agglutinative, suffixing and compounding' (abstract p.3) — the only pre-root material is three low-frequency reduplicative 'pre-bases' (ATT RED.elp, FREQ RED.ep, PL RED.ew-, §2.6.2 p.62, §3.7.4 p.87).

evidence_works.detail: Vowel-initial branch of the catalog rule (01, 010, 0100...) confirmed exactly: V-initial words stress the second syllable regardless of length (examples up to 7 syllables, e.g. /i:tatari:tatara/ [i.'dA.tA.ri.dA.tA.r(A)] 'willy wag tail'). morph.rootq: "The syllabic canon of Amara is: (C1) V (C2) ... Primary stress occurs on the penultimate syllabic vowel." (Thurston 1996:205). The rule is stated over the word with no reference to root or stem, and the stress-marked transcriptions on the same page show the count running over prefixes and proclitics: am-ri [ámbri] 'you (plural) bathe' (stress on the subject prefix), ka oŋgup [kóŋgup] 'his coconut to eat', ne akai [nákai] 'with a stick', i-pon ne eiki [iponéiki] 'it's full of water'.
morph.elicq: The one-sentence stress statement (p.205) gives no evidential basis. The data are from elicitation fieldwork with a primary informant: 'to Mr. Peter Lingaso of Kimbe village who acted as the primary informant for Amara' (p.197 fn.2); 'Endolexical items were generally easy to elicit from Amara speakers, but during elicitation sessions, the call for ectolexical items usually stimulated a lengthy discussion, frequently in Kabana' (p.201); lexicon 'based primarily on data collected [in] 1981 and 1982 ... updated through written correspondence ... and a brief period of research in 1988' (p.217). Stress-marked transcriptions on p.205 include short phrases ([iponéiki], [nákai]) as well as single…
morph.stmt: Thurston gives no one-line typological label; his outline shows a split profile: 'The seven pronominal distinctions occur with 3 paradigms: (1) the focal (disjunctive) pronouns, (2) the prefixes used to indicate verbal subjects, and (3) the suffixes used, primarily, to indicate possession with inalienable nouns' (p.206) -- i.e. verbal inflection is exclusively prefixal (subject person-number A-, k-, i-, tA-, am-, kA-, ki-; unproductive causative pa-), nominal person marking is suffixal, derivation is circumfixal/suffixal (nominal prefix A- + nominaliser -ŋo, adjectival -ŋe), and tense, aspect, mood, negation and polar interrogation are not affixal at all…

The section opens impressionistically: "Stress is manifested as a slight increase in the loudness and a slight raising in the pitch of the stressed syllable in comparison with neighbouring unstressed syllables. For some speakers, or in some styles of speech, either the vowel and/or the consonantal coda of the stressed syllable may be slightly longer than in unstressed syllables" (§2.5 p.24); word-level examples are cited as isolated transcribed words, and phrase-level stress is treated 'only briefly' with one sentence example (42) p.27. morph.stmt: Anejom̃ is mildly affixing and mixed: nouns take prefixes (definite/singular n-/in-, nominaliser n-, plural elpu-, dual o-, collectives, nef(e)- 'big', nev(e)- 'which', nalve- DIM) and, apart from possessive/construct suffixes, essentially no suffixes ("The only nominal suffix so far recorded (apart from the possessive suffixes) appears to be the not very productive form -mii", §3.3.6 p.53); verbs take a few semi-productive prefixes (awo- CAUS, ehev(a)- 'how', imy(i)- COM, er(i)- MUT, ec- MULT, echo-subject proclitic m-) and suffixes for transitivity/object (-i, -ñ, -c, -n), direction/location (-jai, -se, -pam, -pan, -kou...) and politeness (-sjak), while subject person, tense, aspect…

11.sec_rule: Secondary (weaker) stress on every second syllable to the left of the primary stress, iteratively (right-aligned syllabic trochees; Lynch's rule (40)); when primary stress is final on a geminate/long vowel, secondary falls two syllables to its left. E.g. /ˌnalaˈmerai/ 'boiling', /eˌtʃhapeˈsiraɣ/, /ˌalŋauˈñiː/ 'cross over', /ˌθuːkˈθuːk/ 'squeak'.

evidence_works.detail: Earlier first-hand sketch by the same author as the entry's source (Lynch 2000). States, tentatively, that primary stress 'appears to fall on the penultimate syllable, with geminate vowels counting as two syllables' (exx. (9), e.g. /nefalañ/ 'road', /ecjii/ 'to comb') and that 'There is some evidence, however, that primary stress falls on the antepenultimate syllable if the antepenultimate and penultimate syllables of a word contain the same vocalic elements and are separated by a single consonant' (exx. (10): /itiyi/ negative particle, /elehel/ 'blow, of wind', /inlilitai/ 'bush', /inmunuka/ 'thunder'). Says nothing about secondary stress; closes 'Stress is, however, one more area of Anejom phonology that requires considerably more attention' (p. 100). Also records that 'Neither Capell nor Hewitt treats stress at all' (p. 99).

sources.text: "The occurrence of stress remains to be fully analysed, but in general, it tends to occur most frequently in penultimate position on isolated words. This, however, is subject to other rules in which the stress is moved from one syllable to another as the result of conditioning by other morphemes. For example, /ádo/ 'sun' has stress on the first syllable when uttered alone, but on the second when immediately preceding /nîŋê/ ... Stress is not attested as phonemic." (Thurston 1982:92)

morph.stmt: Anêm is affixally two-sided but asymmetric by word class: every finite verb carries an obligatory portmanteau subject prefix (person/number/gender/realis-irrealis; plus the gê-/kê- verbalising prefix), while all other inflection is suffixal — object, possessor and prepositional-object pronominal suffixes with their class consonants, plural-subject -îl, reflexive -m, reciprocal -ak — and nouns take no prefixes at all. B83 p.21: 'Verbs occur with an obligatory prefix marking subject; no other word classes occur with prefixes.' B83 p.38: 'Anêm possessive affixes are all suffixes.' 13.prule: Stress on the penultimate syllable of every word (2-syllable words: initial; 3-syllable words: penultimate, some words varying penultimate ~ initial, ganj'mada / 'ganjmada); 4-syllable words are stressed initially and on the penult ('maru'wara); in words of five or more syllables stress falls on the penult, on the stem-initial syllable (unless it immediately precedes the penult) and on the word-initial syllable except where the word begins with a single-syllable prefix (unprefixed 'maruwa'rala 10010 vs prefixed a'yilwi'yilwi, dji'walanj'mandji 01010; 'gambala'wuturu'manjdji 10010010). Kirton states no regular primary/secondary distinction among these stresses but calls penultimate stress the 'strong constant'; the rule string shows unprefixed words.
13.srule: In words of four or more syllables the word-initial syllable carries a second stress besides the penult ('maru'wara, 'maruwa'rala); a word beginning with a monosyllabic prefix stresses the stem-initial syllable instead (a'yilwi'yilwi, dji'walanj'mandji); longer prefixed words add a stem-initial stress unless it would abut the penult ('gumba'ramanda'ninja), with a noted tendency toward alternate-syllable stresses preceding the penult ('gumbara'manda'ninjdja). The stresses of a word are not ranked: 'no clear regular distinction between primary and secondary stress'.

morph.elicq: Kirton 1967:25: 'The following rules of stress have been formulated on the basis of predictable stress behaviour and on the basis of trends noted'; note 1, p.27: 'The analysis of this paper was done on data obtained during 12 months' field work at Borroloola under the auspices of the Summer Institute of Linguistics.' morph.stmt: Yanyuwa is heavily affixing on both sides with a prefixal person/class system and suffixal case/TAM: 'All verbs have both prefixes and suffixes... Prefixes carry meanings of negative, indicative mood, recurrative aspect, reflexive or non-reflexive voice, and distinguish nominative and ergative person functions. Suffixes distinguish conversative and recountive mood orientation, past, present and future tense' (Kirton 1978:6); the verb is 'potentially consisting of five prefixes, a verb stem and three suffixes' (Kirton & Charlie 1996:4), and 'Nouns normally take both class-case-marker prefixes and case suffixes' (1996:11); Yanyuwa was traditionally classified as a 'prefixing' language…

qtr.text: Utterances in Apalai can be segmented into words that are meaningful both as grammatical and as phonological units. From the phonological point of view, the word is a sequence of syllables in which the penultimate is stressed: parúru 'banana'. There is a small number of words with only one syllable. These may receive the intensive stress depending on their position in larger constructions: tám 'grandfather'. ... The stress patterns, however, are never contrastive. Thus it is not necessary to symbolise the intensive stress in the phonemic spelling.

14.quote: As enunciações em Apalai podem ser segmentadas em palavras que são significativas tanto como unidades gramaticais quanto fonológicas. Do ponto de vista fonológico, a palavra e uma seqüência de sílabas em que a penúltima é acentuada: parúru "banana". Há um pequeno número de palavras com uma só sílaba. Estas podem receber o acento intensivo dependendo de sua posição em construções maiores: tám "avô". ... Os padrões acentuais, porém, nunca são contrastivos. 14.sec_rule: Secondary stress on closed syllables and on nasal-vowel syllables adjacent to at least one unstressed syllable (kòntapanónko 'getting cold', emè'nónko 'daybreak'); it may also fall on the initial syllable of words of four or more syllables when the second syllable is unstressed (xìrikazúru 'grass'). Placement is somewhat flexible when these factors interact; never contrastive.
14.sec_quote: O acento secundário cai em sílabas travadas e em sílabas nasais contíguas a pelo menos uma sílaba não-acentuada: kòntapanónko "ficando frio", emè'nónko "romper do dia". O acento secundário pode cair na sílaba inicial das palavras de quatro ou mais sílabas quando a segunda sílaba não e acentuada: xírikazúru "grama". [...] Os padrões acentuais, porém, nunca são contrastivos.

secx.sec_quote_tr: Secondary stress falls on closed syllables and on nasal syllables adjacent to at least one unstressed syllable: kòntapanónko 'getting cold', emè'nónko 'daybreak'. Secondary stress may fall on the initial syllable of words of four or more syllables when the second syllable is not stressed: xírikazúru 'grass'. [...] The stress patterns, however, are never contrastive.

sources.text: "In Apinajé, stress falls invariably on the last syllable of the phonological word. ... Stress is a necessary and sufficient property of the phonological word, and is indicative of its boundaries. ... In examples (72-74), stress falls predictably on the last syllable regardless of the word length." (Oliveira 2005: 71). Also p. 73 on compounds: "primary stress falls on the last syllable of the compound. ... the word-final clitic always takes primary stress regardless of whether it is an odd or even syllable."

Stress is a necessary and sufficient property of the phonological word, and is indicative of its boundaries. However, the limits of a phonological word sometimes do not coincide with those of a grammatical wor…
15.dloc: Oliveira 2005, The Language of the Apinajé People of Central Brazil (U. Oregon diss.), Ch. II §3 'Stress system', p. 71; open copy: http://etnolinguistica.wdfiles.com/local--files/tese%3Aoliveira-2005/oliveira_2005.pdf
15.srule: Secondary stress is stated only for compounds and base+clitic formations (the clitics ti 'AUG' and ɾɛ 'DIM' 'bear independent stress'), which Oliveira analyses as phonological phrases containing more than one phonological word (p. 100): 'the original stress properties of the bases tend to be somewhat reflected in the derived word, even though primary stress falls on the last syllable of the compound... Overall secondary stress falls on the last syllable of the first base'; in compounds of monosyllabic bases 'every first and third syllables left-to-right take on stress; the word-final clitic always takes primary stress' (p. 73); the compound pattern is 'an iambic stress pattern, parsed from right to left, with final prominence, foot construction being iterative' (p. 101). Simple lexical bases (72-74) carry a single final stress.
15.quote: In Apinajé, stress falls invariably on the last syllable of the phonological word. Morphemes are typically short, such that it is common for monomorphemic words to be one-syllable long. ... Stress is a necessary and sufficient property of the phonological word, and is indicative of its boundaries. However, the limits of a phonological word sometimes do not coincide with those of a grammatical word (see section III.2.2). In examples (72-74), stress falls predictably on the last syllable regardless of the word length.

15.sec_rule: Only in compounds: within the simple phonological word there is one (final) stress; in compounds each lexical base and the stress-bearing clitics (ti 'AUG', ɾɛ 'DIM') keep a stress, primary on the compound-final syllable and secondary on the last syllable of each earlier base ('Overall secondary stress falls on the last syllable of the first base'; compounds show 'an iambic stress pattern, parsed from right to left, with final prominence, foot construction being iterative').
15.sec_quote: primary stress falls on the last syllable of the compound. In (77.a), the elements of the compound are, respectively, a disyllabic and a monosyllabic base. Overall secondary stress falls on the last syllable of the first base. ... Every first and third syllables left-to-right take on stress; the word-final clitic always takes primary stress regardless of whether it is an odd or even syllable.

secx.primary_revised_quote: Na língua apinayé, cada palavra de mais de uma sílaba possui um acento de liberdade limitada, que pode recair nas duas últimas sílabas da palavra. Ressaltamos, entretanto, que na maioria das palavras da língua Apinayé, o acento recai na última sílaba. [Engl.: each polysyllabic word has one stress, of limited freedom, on either of the last two syllables; in most words on the last.]

16.dq: Arabana-Wangkangurru follows the majority of Australian languages in having a strong stress accent on the first syllable of a word. There are no monosyllabics (except for Eastern Wangkangurru ko 'yes'); in words of two or three syllables there is simply the one accent falling on the first syllable.
16.dloc: Hercus 1994:47 §2.12 (archive.org scan, by the owner review); clitic sentence
16.prule: Primary stress falls on the first syllable of every word (there are no monosyllables except Eastern Wangkangurru ko 'yes'); Aranda loans follow the same rule.
16.srule: Secondary stress on the third, fifth and seventh syllables of longer (4+-syllable) words, i.e. alternate syllables after the initial main stress (kátharùngka, Yúrkunàngku); in long polymorphemic words this is superseded by a morphological rule: each bound morpheme of two or three syllables takes a secondary accent on its first syllable (kúdna-tyúrra-àpu-kànha, kátha-nàngka-lìparna). Polysyllabic clitic particles also carry a secondary accent (disyllabic on the first, trisyllabic on the second syllable, §7.1.1 p. 247).
16.quote: Arabana-Wangkangurru follows the majority of Australian languages in having a strong stress accent on the first syllable of a word. There are no monosyllabics (except for Eastern Wangkangurru ko 'yes'); in words of two or three syllables there is simply the one accent falling on the first syllable.
16.idn: Arabana-Wangkangurru (Arabana: Arabana proper/Piltapalta, Wangkakupa, Midlaliri; Wangkangurru: Simpson Desert Wangkangurru, Marlu-papu-nganha/Wangkatyaka, Eastern Wangkangurru) (the source treats Arabana [Glottolog arab1267] and Wangkangurru [wang1290] as one language, 'Arabana-Wangkangurru', and states the accent rule for the whole); data: North-east of South Australia west and north of Lake Eyre…
16.exq_: There are however two situations in which this whole system is ignored. One is in exclamations, vocatives, and imperatives that are shouted ... These always have the main accent on the final syllable ... The other exceptional circumstance is in song, where any syllable can be stressed

evidence_works.detail: Primary stress fixed on the first syllable; secondary on 3rd/5th/7th syllables in long monomorphemic words, which matches the catalog rule string exactly. Refinement: in polymorphemic words a morphological rule supersedes the odd-syllable count (each bound morpheme of 2-3 syllables carries a secondary accent on its first syllable, e.g. katha-rnda-nangka-lipama), so the catalog's alternating pattern is only the default for long simple words. Exceptions: shouted exclamations/vocatives/imperatives take main accent on the final syllable; song allows any syllable, esp. the final; compound nouns hav

17.srule: Secondary stresses on the initial syllable and on every second syllable after it, i.e. on the heads of all non-final trochees counted from the left edge (tenakari 2ndary syll. 1, primary 3; samaru 1/3; huwahaniya 1, 3/5; sapohosano 1, 3/4) - Topintzi 2006 after Payne & Rich 1988. [If the record stays on Rich 1963: 'Rich 1963:201-203 does not rank word stresses as primary vs secondary; phrase-medial words carry up to three lexically placed stresses ('ka'hi, 'kiya'tu vs 'ki'yatu, 'na'pana'ha, 'saka'mana'ha).']
17.quote: In describing the stress patterns for Arabela words, S. will be used to represent a syllable. One-syllable words in my data are all stressed. Two-syllable words have the following stress patterns: (1) 'S.S /'kama../ 'uncle' (2) 'S.'S /'ka'hi../ 'axe' (3) S.'S /..ri'tya../ 'quick' (4) S.S (only one word noted with this pattern) /..ryunu../ 'boil'. Three-syllable words have the following patterns: (1) 'S.S.'S /'kiya'tu../ 'my daughter' (2) 'S.'S.S /'ki'yatu../ 'a type of fish' (3) 'S.S.S /'tariki../ 'morning' (4) S.'S.S /..ru'paynyu../ 'to stick'.

evidence_works.detail: Acoustic thesis on Arabela segments, six speakers (three men, three women; Table 8, p. 88), Zoom H4n + head-mounted Shure SM35 (p. 91), Praat script extracting F0, F1, F2 at 30 % of each vowel plus duration. Material: Spanish-prompted single words, each pronounced three times on its own and then once inside the carrier sentence 'Yo digo la palabra [X] en mi casa' (from 2016; 2015 sessions used speaker-made sentences), p. 90-91: 'indicamos al colaborador que debe pronunciar tres veces la palabra objetivo. Por último, se le pidió que pronunciara la oración modelo con la palabra objetivo dentro una sola vez.' Stress enters only as a variable for vowel quality and duration: 235 bisyllabic CV.CV words with open syllables and obstruent-adjacent vowels, 'instruimos a un script que separe a vocales acentuadas y no acentuadas' (p. 111), the basis of the stressed/unstressed labelling and which tokens (isolated or carrier) were used are not stated. Findings: stressed vowels 'un poco más extremas' in the F1/F2 space with unstressed ones centralising, except [i] in men and [a] in women (p. 114), and stressed vowels 0.010-0.040 s longer than unstressed in both sexes (p. 119). The only placement statement is the aside on p. 107 justifying why Table 9 pools stressed and unstressed vowels: 'el acento tiende a ubicarse en la última sílaba'. This is not an analysis of word stress and the thesis never engages Rich 1963 or Rich 1999 on stress; the entry's cfw already names it as a passing remark consistent with Rich 1963's phrase-final stress rule (isolated words are phrase-final), and the procedure confirms that three of the four tokens per word were isolated words.

22.dq: Stress is right-aligned to a domain. At the word-level it is trochaic and weight sensitive, while at the stem-level it is simply final. There is no iteration of stress, though clash-avoidance creates the percept of rhythmic alternation. | Stress in Mapudungun is non-contrastive.

22.heavy: Closed syllable (the maximum syllable is CVC): 'In general, closed syllables tend to attract stress. Words ending in a consonant are stressed on the final syllable' (Sadowsky et al. 2013:94); 'Las sílabas cerradas atraen el acento principal: kurám, máñke' (Zúñiga 2006:64). Not called weight by Sadowsky; Molineaux 2023:21 calls word-level stress 'trochaic and weight sensitive'.
22.dflt: penult when neither of the last two syllables is closed (Zúñiga 2006:64: femngéchi; Sadowsky et al. 2013:94, trisyllables: [mɜˈwɪθɜ]); in open-open disyllables final or penult by dialect (kachú; northern final, southern penult), and Sadowsky applies these disyllable rules to the last two syllables of words of four or more syllables
22.prule: Main stress at the right edge of the word, attracted by closed syllables, stated as tendencies. Sadowsky et al. 2013:94: a word ending in a consonant is stressed on its final syllable; a trisyllable ending in an open syllable is stressed on the penult, otherwise on the final syllable; in words of four or more syllables the disyllable rules apply to the last two syllables; vowel-final disyllables take final stress in northern and north-central dialects and penultimate stress in southern and south-central dialects, a disyllable with a closed first and open second syllable is stressed on the first, one with both syllables closed tends to final stress; 'There may also be some degree of idiolectal variation'. Zúñiga 2006:64: 'El acento principal recae sobre la última o penúltima sílaba de la palabra. Las sílabas cerradas atraen el acento principal'; in polysyllables the penult tends to take the main stress if neither of the last two syllables is closed (femngéchi, but machitún); the verbal suffix -fi attracts the main stress. Molineaux 2023:21: stress 'right-aligned to a domain', 'trochaic and weight sensitive' at the word level, 'simply final' at the stem level, with no iteration.
22.srule: One secondary stress in words of four or more syllables, on the first or second syllable: the closed one if only one of the two is closed, the first if both are open, the second if both are closed (Sadowsky et al. 2013:94); Zúñiga 2006:64 likewise ('un acento secundario, generalmente en la primera o segunda sílaba; aquella que sea cerrada lo atrae'). Molineaux 2023:21 finds no iteration of stress ('clash-avoidance creates the percept of rhythmic alternation'). The alternating even-syllable secondaries of Echeverría & Contreras 1965:134 (the StressTyp2 coding) are not confirmed by later first-hand work.

corr.head: Word stress is stem-initial and secondary to pause-group stress
corr.detail: Gordon (2002) codes word-initial stress (10 100 1000 10000 100000 1000000 10000000), but the source places word stress on the first syllable of the stem — the second syllable of the word when a prefix precedes a consonant-initial stem ([dakábo] 'I am bathing' vs [dákabo] 'I am speaking') — and calls it secondary to a penultimate pause-group stress that tends to predominate in natural speech. The language is listed as morphologically determined, not as a fixed (quantity-insensitive) pattern.

ev.text: Arawak has two partially conflicting stress rules. 1. Each pause group potentially has a stress that falls on the penultimate syllable of that group. Secondary stresses fall on alternate syllables moving backward in the pause group. 2. Each word potentially has a secondary stress which falls on the first syllable of its stem. In natural speech, such as that heard in recorded conversations and stories, both rules operate simultaneously in determining the actual position of stress, but pause-group stress tends to be more prominent. In very precise speech of the sort a speaker uses when dictating for transcription or when correcting a linguist, word stress tends to predominate. In this latter …

23.prule: Word stress on the first syllable of the stem: word-initial for unprefixed words and for prefix + vowel-initial stem (after vowel-cluster reduction, [dákabo] 'I am speaking'), second syllable of the word for prefix + consonant-initial stem ([dakábo] 'I am bathing'). Separately, each pause group (roughly the phrase, fn. 4) has a primary stress on its penultimate syllable with secondaries on alternate syllables moving backward; in natural speech both rules operate and the pause-group stress tends to be more prominent, while in very precise speech (dictating for transcription, correcting a linguist) word stress tends to predominate.
23.srule: Secondary stresses fall on alternate syllables moving leftward from the penultimate (pause-group) primary; in addition every word has a stress on the first syllable of its stem (word-level, morphologically placed); suffixes never take word stress; epenthetic -da can be added to avoid two adjacent stressed syllables.

evidence_works.note: The only stress statement in the book is de Goeje's 1928 field note, reproduced in French translation in the appendix 'Information recueillie au Surinam en 1907 et en 1928' (Suriname material from Johannes Baptist and two women consultants), p. 358: 'L'accent a été marqué aussi bien que possible, il est indiqué par «, ». Remarquons toutefois que les mots, les phrases et les textes ont été prononcés dans des conditions particulières et anormales, et que l'accentuation peut en avoir été influencée. Ceci explique probablement que dans les mots prononcés séparément, l'accent marque souvent la première syllabe, même lorsque c'est un préfixe pronominal (c'est également le cas dans le vocabulaire de Sm.). Apparemment, les suffixes tels que -Ci-, -tu-, -li, etc., ne sont jamais accentués.' Patte's own descriptive part and dictionaries mark only vowel length (circumflex; p. 13: 'La longueur vocalique est indiquée par un accent circonflexe') and give no stress rule; the 'accent (li)' diacritic she mentions on p. 19 describes Schumann's Moravian transcription, not her own analysis. Detail added to the entry: an independent 1907/1928 Suriname observation that words pronounced in isolation often carry stress on the first syllable even when that syllable is a pronominal prefix, and that the suffixes -Ci-, -tu-, -li are never stressed; de Goeje himself attributes the initial placement to abnormal elicitation conditions. This sits beside Pet 2011's account that in very precise (dictation) speech word stress predominates and falls on the first syllable of the stem, and it is consistent with the older word-initial codings that the entry's corr[0] discusses; the 'even when it is a pronominal prefix' remark diverges slightly from Pet's stem-initial rule but is an impressionistic, self-caveated note, not evidence to recode.

tn.quote: 2.1.2. Сверхсегментные признаки обычно не проявляются в отдельности, а выступают в комбинациях разного типа, причем просодические особенности не являются релевантными признаками для дифференциации фонем и придают им лишь дополнительную фонетическую окраску. … Частота основного тона для проявления словесного ударения имеет дополнительную значимость, тональность, в основном, связана с проявлением фразового ударения и типами предложений по характеру семантико-синтаксического содержания.
tn.translation: 2.1.2. Suprasegmental features usually do not appear in isolation but occur in combinations of various types; prosodic properties are not relevant features for the differentiation of phonemes and give them only additional phonetic colouring. … Fundamental frequency has (only) supplementary significance for the manifestation of word stress; tonality (pitch) is mainly connected with the manifestation of phrasal stress and with sentence types according to their semantic-syntactic content.

26.prule: No catalog-legal corrected rule exists. The source's actual system (Voorhoeve 1965 §§40-44) is: regular alternation of accented and unaccented vowels; monomorphematic 2V words 01 "as a rule" with a listed 10 exception class and apparent minimal pairs, 3V words 101 with final accent strongest "as a rule" (exception canupir 010); polymorphematic words place the FIRST accent on V1 if the first morpheme has one vowel (§42 rule 1, with a listed counter-class jis.mak etc.) and on V2 if it has two (§42 rule 2), alternating rightward with licensed two-unaccented-vowel lapses in specified morphological configurations (§44), and imperatives/shouted forms always final-accented (§44.3). This rule takes the morphological parse as input, so it is not a function of syllable count and cannot be stated as a catalog pattern (fails our criterion 1 on its face).
26.srule: Stated (Voorhoeve 1965 §§40-44): accented and unaccented vowels alternate regularly, so words of three or more vowels carry more than one accent. Three-vowel monomorphemic words: accents on V1 and V3, the last 'as a rule' the stronger, i.e. V1 = weaker accent (úsawíc 'banana'; exception canupir). Polymorphemic words: the first accent falls on V1 if the first morpheme has one vowel, on V2 if it has two; further accents follow by alternation, with lapses of two unaccented vowels in listed morpheme configurations (tów.om.iw.tám 1001) and obligatory final accent in imperatives and shouted -a forms; which accent is strongest in polymorphemic words is not stated (4-vowel words attested 1010 ó.sirím.tak, 0101 emén.metén, 1001).

evidence_works.work: Drabbe 1963, Drie Asmat-dialecten (Verhandelingen KITLV 42: pp. 13, 48, 95)
evidence_works.detail: Grammar of three other Central Asmat dialects (Kawenak as spoken at Ajam, Keenok at Amor, Keenakap at Ndamen; informants named with ages, book pp. 3-4). Stress is treated in one note, p. 13 (par. 9 Aantekening): 'De klemtoon valt in tweelettergr. woorden op de laatste lettergr., in drielettergr. woorden op de eerste. Wanneer een woord een andere klemtoon heeft, is dat een teken dat het een levende of een versteende samenst. is. Zulk een klemtoon geven we aan met een accent grave, bv. èpetsj oudere broer, een versteende samenst, zie 123.' Par. 123 (p. 95) applies this to kinship terms with initial stress in Kw and Kp, analysed as fossilised compounds whose first member no longer occurs on its own. Par. 62 (p. 48), on indicative verb forms: 'In alle boven gegeven vormen hoort men een zwakke klemtoon op het laatste suffix, en wanneer het suffixencomplex bestaat uit meer dan één lettergr. bovendien nog een gelijkwaardige klemt. op de laatste lettergr. van de ww.st.' No minimal pairs and no instrumental data; the same final default for disyllables as Voorhoeve 1965 par. 41; the trisyllable statement (initial only) differs from Voorhoeve's 'first and third, the last stronger'; deviant stress is explained as (fossilised) compounding, which is Voorhoeve's 'morphological structure' factor under another name.

sources.text: "12.2 Dakota Accent Rule (DAR): Primary stress is assigned by the Dakota Accent Rule (DAR), as described and motivated in Shaw (1980:31-44). ... The rule states that primary stress is assigned to the second syllable of a word unless there is only one syllable, in which case primary stress is assigned to that syllable. As a consequence of this rule, primary stress never falls beyond the second syllable. Primary stress moves leftwards as prefixes are added to a word." (Cumberland 2005:57)

28.dq: In Assyrian, stress is expiratory and normally is placed on the penultimate. It is not shifted in verb suffixation (i.e. is goes to the newly formed penultimate). Stress often affects the quality and length of vowels; it may cause the ommission of vowels and, at times, of entire syllables. (Tsereteli 1978)

(5) When the 2nd pl. pronominal affix -ōxun, or the plural imperative affix -ūn are added, the accent is often on the antepenultimate. 29.cfw: Goderich 2020, a phonology of seven Atayal dialects from the author's own fieldwork, finds stress always word-final and attributes the penultimate stress heard by Li 1981 to a rising pitch on the penult, with Lambert 1999 (acoustically, for Mabalay) and Lin 2015 (Squliq) agreeing, but Rau 1992, a reference grammar of Wulai Squliq, gives penultimate stress in long-vowel stems and final stress only in the rest, so one authoritative older description contradicts the final-stress reading. One further first-hand description conflicts (see the conflicting-description item); the entry follows Goderich 2020.

31.srule: In polysyllabic words whose first and penultimate syllables are not adjacent (four or more syllables), primary stress usually falls on the penult and secondary stress on the first syllable: /'ate"paye/ far out!, /'orkewey"naywo/ four, /'periya"yawnow/ grass (Feldman 1986:15); disyllables carry a single initial stress.
31.quote: By and large, main word stress ... tends to fall on the first syllable of an Awtuw word. There is also a tendency towards penultimate stress. Where the two tendencies coincide, on disyllabic words, the stress pattern is regular. ... Where the two tendencies do not coincide, but the first and penultimate syllables are not adjacent, in polysyllabic words, primary stress will usually fall on the penult and secondary stress on the first syllable. ... There are, however, a number of exceptions to this generalisation among words other than verbs, while verbs do not appear to follow it at all.

31.sec_rule: Secondary stress on the first syllable in words of four or more syllables (first and penult not adjacent), with primary on the penult: /'orkewey"naywo/ 'four', /'ate"paye/ 'far out!', /'periya"yawnow/ 'grass'. Di- and trisyllables carry a single stress.
31.sec_quote: Where the two tendencies do not coincide, but the first and penultimate syllables are not adjacent, in polysyllabic words, primary stress will usually fall on the penult and secondary stress on the first syllable. /'orkewey"naywo/ four, /'ate"paye/ far out!, /'owtiy"kayaen/ old, /'periya"yawnow/ grass
